concepts.name: Loan concentration risk
concepts.definition: Having large exposures to one borrower, industry, region, asset class or funding source, so a single adverse shock causes large losses. It can sit on either side of the balance sheet (Penn Square: assets; SVB: deposits plus long-duration securities).
misconceptions: Thinking concentration only exists on the asset side

questions.prompt: What is loan concentration risk?
options: Having large exposures to one borrower, industry, region, asset class or funding source, so one adverse shock causes big losses
The risk that any single borrower defaults
The risk that market interest rates change
Holding too many small loans to manage efficiently
questions.explanation: Concentration risk is about exposure to a common shock: many exposures that go bad together.
feedback: That's default risk on one loan; concentration is about many exposures sharing a shock.
That's interest rate risk.
Many small, unrelated loans are diversified, the opposite of concentrated.

questions.prompt: In the Penn Square (1982) failure, where was the concentration?
options: Asset side: loans to oil and gas companies
Liability side: deposits from tech and VC firms
questions.explanation: Energy prices fell, oil and gas borrowers couldn't repay, and the loan losses wiped out capital.
feedback: That was SVB in 2023.
That was part of SVB's problem.
That's the Hungary/Croatia sovereign cases.

questions.prompt: Why did SVB (2023) fail?
options: Rates rose, cutting the value of its long-duration bonds, and a run by its concentrated tech/VC depositors forced it to sell them at a loss
Its loans to oil and gas companies defaulted
Its tech borrowers defaulted on their loans
questions.explanation: SVB's deposits tripled, it had few loans to make, so it bought long-dated bonds. Rate rises cut their value; deposit withdrawals forced sales that turned paper losses into realised ones.
feedback: That's Penn Square.
SVB's problem wasn't loan defaults; its clients didn't need many loans.
That's sovereign risk, not SVB.

questions.prompt: A bank's exposure to a single industry rises. What happens to the loss it would suffer from a shock to that industry?
questions.explanation: More exposure to one sector means a sector-wide shock hits a bigger share of the book.
feedback: Concentrating raises, not lowers, the damage from a common shock.
Exposure size drives the loss.

questions.prompt: SVB's depositors withdraw funds just as rising rates have cut the value of its bond portfolio. What happens to its losses?
options: Paper losses become realised losses because the bank must sell bonds at low prices to pay depositors
The losses disappear because the bonds are held to maturity
Losses fall, because higher rates raise bond prices
No effect: deposits and bonds sit on different sides of the balance sheet
questions.explanation: Rates ↑ → bond values ↓ (paper loss) → deposit run → forced sales → realised losses that eat equity.
feedback: The run is what stopped SVB holding them to maturity.
Higher rates lower existing bond prices.
That's exactly why two-sided concentration is dangerous: the sides feed each other.

questions.prompt: What does SVB show about concentration on BOTH sides of the balance sheet?
options: The two sides feed each other: the asset-side losses only became fatal because the liability-side run forced sales
Asset-side and liability-side concentration always offset each other
questions.explanation: Concentrated depositors (liabilities) plus concentrated long-duration securities (assets): a shock to one forced losses on the other.
feedback: They amplified each other.
Without the bond losses the withdrawals could have been met.
Without the run the bonds could have been held to maturity.

concepts.name: Migration analysis and transition matrices
concepts.definition: Tracking how borrowers move between rating grades. Sort loans by rating, re-rate at year end, and compare with the historical transition matrix; if a sector deteriorates faster than history, curtail lending to it.
misconceptions: Reading the transition matrix's diagonal as default rates

questions.prompt: What does migration analysis track?
options: How borrowers move between rating grades over time
How interest rates move over time
How loans move between bank branches
questions.explanation: A migration is a move from one grade to another, e.g. a downgrade from A to BBB.
feedback: That's interest rate risk.
That's about funding, not credit quality.
Not the meaning of migration here.

questions.prompt: In a transition matrix, the largest number in each row is usually...
options: The probability of staying in the same rating: ratings are 'sticky'
The probability of the rating being withdrawn
questions.explanation: In the Moody's matrix, e.g. 82.52% of Baa issuers are still Baa a year later.
feedback: Default probabilities are small except for the lowest grades.
WR is a single-digit percentage.
Upgrades are a small share of each row.

questions.prompt: Moving down the rating scale (from Aaa towards Caa-C), what happens to the one-year default rate?
questions.explanation: Default risk rises steeply as ratings fall: 0.00% for Aaa versus 12.41% for Caa-C in the Moody's matrix.
feedback: Lower grades default more, not less.
Default rates differ sharply by grade.

questions.prompt: What does 'WR' mean in the Moody's transition matrix?
options: Rating withdrawn: rated at the start of the year but unrated at the end (e.g. debt repaid, firm acquired)
questions.explanation: WR is the share of issuers whose rating was withdrawn during the year; it isn't a default.
feedback: Defaults have their own column.
Caa-C is the lowest grade.
Not a weighting.

questions.prompt: This year 8% of a bank's BBB loans were downgraded, against a historical average of 5%. What should the bank do?
options: Curtail lending to that sector or loan class: it is deteriorating faster than history suggests
Increase lending, because ratings are sticky
Raise its concentration limit for the sector
questions.explanation: Step 3 of migration analysis: compare actual deterioration with the historical matrix and cut lending where it's worse.
feedback: Faster-than-normal downgrades are a warning sign.
Downgrades lower loan values and signal rising PD.
The response is to reduce, not increase, exposure.

questions.prompt: Of 200 loans rated BBB at the start of the year, 170 are still BBB and 10 were upgraded; the rest were downgraded. What share was downgraded?
feedback: That's the upgraded share (10 ÷ 200).
That's the share that moved at all (30 ÷ 200).
That's the share that stayed BBB.

questions.prompt: Using the Moody's matrix, what share of Baa issuers end the year below investment grade (Ba or lower) or in default?
questions.explanation: Ba 4.68% + B 0.61% + Caa-C 0.06% + Default 0.28% = 5.63%. Baa3 is the lowest investment grade, so Ba and below is speculative.
feedback: That's only the move to Ba.
That's only default.
That adds the 7.71% withdrawn (WR), which isn't a downgrade.

questions.prompt: In the lecture's hypothetical matrix, a grade-2 loan has a 0.12 chance of moving to grade 1, 0.83 of staying, 0.03 of moving to grade 3 and 0.02 of defaulting. Of 500 grade-2 loans, how many are expected to deteriorate (to grade 3 or default)?
feedback: That counts only the move to grade 3.
That counts only defaults.
That's 0.17 × 500: everything that leaves grade 2, including upgrades.

concepts.name: Concentration limits
concepts.definition: External limits on the maximum loan size to a borrower, sector or segment (as a % of capital). Concentration limit = Maximum loss as % of capital ÷ Loss rate, where loss rate = 1 − recovery rate. They cap EAD, not PD.
misconceptions: Thinking a higher recovery rate lowers the limit
Capping correlated sectors separately and assuming the risk is gone

questions.prompt: What do concentration limits cap?
options: The maximum exposure (loan size) to a borrower, sector or segment, i.e. EAD, not PD
The interest rate the bank can charge
questions.explanation: Limits restrict how much is on the line; they don't make borrowers less likely to default.
feedback: Limits don't change how likely a borrower is to default.
Not a rate cap.
They apply to lending, not deposits.

questions.prompt: In this formula, what does the loss rate represent?
options: The share of a loan the bank fails to recover if the borrower defaults (1 − recovery rate)
The share of a loan the bank recovers
The maximum loss the bank will accept
questions.explanation: Loss rate = 1 − recovery rate, e.g. 70% recovery gives a 30% loss rate.
feedback: That's the recovery rate; the loss rate is 1 minus it.
That's the numerator.
PD isn't in the formula.
questions.equation: \text{Concentration limit} = \frac{\text{Maximum loss as \% of capital}}{\text{Loss rate}}

questions.prompt: The expected recovery rate on defaulted loans rises. What happens to the concentration limit?
questions.explanation: Higher recovery → lower loss rate (denominator) → higher limit: each dollar lent costs less if it defaults.
feedback: A smaller denominator makes the limit bigger.
The loss rate depends on the recovery rate.
questions.equation: \text{Concentration limit} = \frac{\text{Maximum loss as \% of capital}}{\text{Loss rate}}

questions.prompt: An FI sets a maximum loss of 2% of capital and a concentration limit of 25% for a firm. What is the implied loss rate?
questions.explanation: 25% = 2% ÷ loss rate → loss rate = 0.02 ÷ 0.25 = 8%.
feedback: That's 0.25 ÷ 0.5; divide the maximum loss by the limit.

questions.prompt: A bank's concentration limit is 20% of capital and its expected recovery on defaulted loans is 70%. What maximum loss does it permit, as a % of capital?
questions.explanation: Maximum loss = limit × loss rate = 0.20 × (1 − 0.70) = 0.06.
feedback: That uses the recovery rate (0.20 × 0.70) instead of the loss rate.

questions.prompt: Why does the lecture recommend aggregate limits for industries such as real estate, residential and construction?
options: Their performance is highly correlated, so they tend to fail together
questions.explanation: Separate caps on correlated sectors don't stop them all going bad at once, so they're capped together.
feedback: Profitability isn't the reason.
They're restricted, not banned.
They're usually secured.

questions.prompt: Expected recovery falls from 70% to 40%, and the maximum loss the bank accepts is unchanged. What happens to the concentration limit?
questions.explanation: The loss rate doubles from 30% to 60%, and it's in the denominator, so the limit halves.
feedback: A higher loss rate lowers the limit.
Work through the loss rate: 0.3 → 0.6 doubles it.
The limit depends on the loss rate.
questions.equation: \text{Concentration limit} = \frac{\text{Maximum loss as \% of capital}}{\text{Loss rate}}

questions.prompt: A bank accepts a maximum loss of 3% of capital and expects 60% recovery on defaults. What concentration limit should it set?
feedback: That divides by the recovery rate (0.60) instead of the loss rate.
That multiplies by the loss rate.
That multiplies by the recovery rate.

questions.prompt: A bank caps real estate, residential and construction lending at 10% of capital each. Why might its true concentration risk still be high?
options: These sectors are highly correlated, so separate caps limit concentration in form but not in substance
Because each cap is too low
Because limits change PD rather than EAD
Because geographical limits always override sector limits
questions.explanation: Correlated sectors fail together, so three 10% caps behave like one 30% exposure. Measuring correlation directly is what MPT adds; concentration limits were also criticised as arbitrary.
feedback: The issue is correlation, not the level of each cap.
Limits cap EAD; they don't change PD.
Geographic limits are an extra tool, not an override.

concepts.name: Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT) for loan portfolios
concepts.definition: Portfolio return is a weighted average of loan returns; portfolio variance adds weighted variances plus covariance terms. Diversification reduces risk when loans' default risks are imperfectly correlated (ρ < 1). The minimum risk portfolio has the lowest variance for a given return; efficient portfolios lie on the upper frontier.
misconceptions: Thinking correlation changes expected portfolio return

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental lesson of MPT for a bank's loan book?
options: Credit risk can be reduced by diversification when loans' default risks are not perfectly correlated
Concentrate lending in the loans with the highest return
questions.explanation: A bank is like an investor choosing loan weights to maximise return while minimising risk.
feedback: That ignores risk.
Diversification reduces risk; return is a weighted average.
Correlation is what drives the diversification benefit.

questions.prompt: The correlation between two loans falls. What happens to the portfolio's expected return?
questions.explanation: Expected return is a weighted average of the loans' returns; correlation never appears in it.
feedback: Correlation affects risk, not expected return.
Correlation affects risk, not expected return.
It's still the weighted average.

questions.prompt: Which term in this equation can be negative?
options: 2X₁X₂ρ₁₂σ₁σ₂, when the correlation ρ₁₂ is negative
questions.explanation: Weights and standard deviations are positive, so only ρ can flip a sign, and ρ only appears in the covariance term.
feedback: Squares are never negative.
Squares are never negative.
The covariance term is negative when ρ < 0.

questions.prompt: The correlation between the default risks of two loans falls. What happens to the portfolio's risk?
questions.explanation: Lower correlation → smaller (or negative) covariance term → lower portfolio variance.
feedback: Lower correlation means more diversification, not less.
Portfolio variance depends on ρ.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum risk portfolio?
options: The combination of assets with the lowest variance for a given expected return
The portfolio with the highest expected return
A portfolio holding only risk-free assets
questions.explanation: Many mixes can hit a target return; the minimum risk one does it with the lowest variance.
feedback: That ignores risk.
It's built from risky assets.
One loan gives no diversification.

questions.prompt: Portfolios A and B have the same expected return, but A has higher risk. Which statement is correct?
options: B is efficient (on the frontier); A is inefficient
A is efficient because it's riskier
questions.explanation: For the same return, the lower-risk portfolio dominates; efficient portfolios lie on the upper half of the curve.
feedback: Extra risk without extra return is inefficient.
Only the lower-risk one is efficient.
Same return makes them directly comparable.

questions.prompt: Bank of USYD holds two loans: X = 0.55 and 0.45, returns 8% and 10%. What is the portfolio's expected return?
feedback: That's a simple average; use the weights.
That adds the returns.
That's loan 1 only.

questions.prompt: If two loans' default risks were perfectly correlated (ρ = 1), what would the portfolio's standard deviation equal?
options: The weighted average of the two loans' standard deviations: no diversification benefit
Less than either loan's standard deviation
The sum of the two standard deviations
questions.explanation: With ρ = 1 the variance becomes (X₁σ₁ + X₂σ₂)², so σp = X₁σ₁ + X₂σ₂.
feedback: Zero risk would need perfect negative correlation and the right weights.
That needs ρ < 1.
The weights still apply.

questions.prompt: Bank of USYD: X = 0.55/0.45, σ = 8.55%/9.15%, ρ₁₂ = 0.24. What is the portfolio's standard deviation?
feedback: That's the weighted average of σ, which assumes ρ = 1.
That leaves out the covariance term (ρ = 0).
That's the variance, not its square root.

concepts.name: Moody's KMV Portfolio Manager model
concepts.definition: Builds MPT inputs for non-traded loans: Rᵢ = AISᵢ − EDFᵢ × LGDᵢ; σᵢ = √(EDFᵢ(1 − EDFᵢ)) × LGDᵢ (unexpected loss); ρᵢⱼ from the correlation of borrowers' asset returns (industry, geography, time).
misconceptions: Thinking AIS affects a loan's risk
Forgetting the square root in σᵢ

questions.prompt: Why does the KMV model need special estimates for MPT's inputs on loans?
options: Loans don't trade, so there's no price history to estimate their return, risk and correlation
Loans are too small to matter
MPT can only be used for shares by law
questions.explanation: KMV builds return, risk and correlation from what the bank knows: spread, default probability and likely loss.
feedback: Size isn't the issue.
Default risk is exactly what it models.
MPT applies to any portfolio.

questions.prompt: In this equation, what is AIS?
options: The all-in spread: annual fees + (loan rate − the bank's funding cost)
questions.explanation: AIS is what the bank earns above its own cost of funds if the borrower repays.
feedback: That's EDF.
That's LGD.
That's EDF × LGD.
questions.equation: R_i = AIS_i(1 - EDF_i) + (AIS_i - LGD_i)\,EDF_i = AIS_i - EDF_i \times LGD_i

questions.prompt: LGD doubles and EDF is unchanged. What happens to the loan's risk σᵢ?
questions.explanation: σᵢ is proportional to LGD.
feedback: LGD isn't squared here.
A bigger LGD means more risk.
σᵢ depends on LGD.

questions.prompt: A loan's AIS rises (higher fees), with EDF and LGD unchanged. What happens to its risk σᵢ?
questions.explanation: AIS shifts both outcomes (repaid and defaulted) up equally, so the spread between them doesn't change. AIS only raises Rᵢ.
feedback: AIS isn't in the σᵢ formula.
AIS isn't in the σᵢ formula.

questions.prompt: SydneySide Bank: a loan earns 2% fees and a 4% spread over its cost of funds; LGD is 20% and EDF is 3%. What is the expected return Rᵢ?
feedback: That's AIS; subtract the expected loss.
That subtracts EDF alone instead of EDF × LGD.
That's the expected loss.

questions.prompt: Same SydneySide loan (EDF 3%, LGD 20%). What is its risk σᵢ?
feedback: That forgets to multiply by LGD.
That forgets the square root.
That's the expected loss, not the unexpected loss.

questions.prompt: A loan's EDF rises from 3% to 6% (still well below 50%). What happens to its risk σᵢ?
questions.explanation: EDF(1 − EDF) rises towards its peak at EDF = 50%, so the outcome becomes less predictable and σᵢ rises.
feedback: Below 50%, a higher EDF raises EDF(1 − EDF).
σᵢ depends on EDF.

questions.prompt: Two loans: loan 1 is 60% of the portfolio with R₁ = 6.25%; loan 2 is 40% with R₂ = 5.60%. What is the portfolio return?
feedback: That's a simple average; use the weights.
That's the weighted AIS, before expected losses.
That's loan 1 alone.

questions.prompt: Same two loans: σ₁ = 4.265%, σ₂ = 2.80%, weights 0.6/0.4, ρ₁₂ = −0.25. What is the portfolio's risk σp?
feedback: That uses ρ = +0.25: the sign matters.
That's the weighted average of σ (ρ = 1).
That's the variance, not σ.

questions.prompt: Why is the risk of the two-loan portfolio (2.52%) lower than the risk of either loan on its own?
options: The loans' defaults are negatively correlated, so the covariance term is negative and subtracts from portfolio variance
Because the portfolio's expected return is lower
Because LGD falls when loans are combined
Because the weights add up to one
questions.explanation: ρ < 0 → covariance term negative → σp² falls below the weighted individual variances → σp < each σᵢ.
feedback: Return doesn't determine risk here.
Each loan keeps its LGD.
Weights always sum to one; that alone doesn't cut risk.

concepts.name: Loan volume model
concepts.definition: A partial application of MPT: compare the bank's loan mix with a national benchmark. σⱼ = √(Σ(Xᵢⱼ − Xᵢ)² ÷ N); the bigger the deviation, the more concentrated the bank relative to the benchmark.
misconceptions: Thinking a single σⱼ tells you whether the bank is unusually concentrated without comparing peers

questions.prompt: How does the loan volume model measure concentration?
options: By comparing the bank's loan allocation with a national benchmark: bigger deviations mean more concentration
By regressing sector losses on total loan losses
By counting the number of borrowers
questions.explanation: It's a partial application of MPT that only needs loan shares by category.
feedback: That's the loan loss ratio model.
That's KMV.
The number of borrowers isn't the measure.

questions.prompt: A bank shifts its loan mix closer to the national benchmark. What happens to σⱼ?
questions.explanation: Smaller gaps (Xᵢⱼ − Xᵢ) mean a smaller σⱼ.
feedback: Moving towards the benchmark shrinks the gaps.
σⱼ is built from the gaps.

questions.prompt: Which source can be aggregated to estimate national loan allocations?
questions.explanation: Benchmark data: call reports, shared national credits (C&I loans by 2-digit SIC code) and commercial databases.
feedback: Not a source of loan allocations.
That's a scoring model.
One bank's data can't give a national mix.

questions.prompt: National mortgage banks hold 60% residential, 15% commercial, 5% international and 20% MBS. A local bank holds 50/30/20/0. What is its σ from the benchmark?
feedback: That's the sum of squared gaps before dividing by N and taking the root.
That's the variance (no square root).
That's √0.095: you forgot to divide by N.

questions.prompt: Using the national benchmark, Bank A's σ is 11.73% and Bank B's is 26.69%. What can you conclude?
options: Bank B deviates more from the national mix, mainly through its heavy concentration in loans to individuals
Bank B must have a higher default rate
questions.explanation: Bank B: 55% individuals vs 15% nationally, and 10% real estate vs 45%. Ranking two banks gives σ meaning.
feedback: A lower σ means closer to the benchmark.
The model measures concentration, not default rates.
Both use the same benchmark, so they can be ranked.

questions.prompt: The national mix is 50% real estate, 30% C&I and 20% individuals (3 categories). A bank holds 70/20/10. What is its σ?
feedback: That takes the root before dividing: √0.06 ÷ 3.
That's the variance.
That's √0.06: divide by N first.

concepts.name: Loan loss ratio model
concepts.definition: Based on CAPM: regress a sector's quarterly loss rate on the total loan loss rate. α is the sector loss rate with no sensitivity to the portfolio; βᵢ is the sector's systematic loss sensitivity. βᵢ > 1 means riskier.

questions.prompt: Which idea is the loan loss ratio model borrowed from?
options: CAPM: a sector's risk is its systematic loss sensitivity to losses on the whole loan book
questions.explanation: It works like a share's beta, but for loan losses instead of returns.
feedback: Altman's Z classifies borrowers.
Duration is about rate sensitivity.
That's sovereign risk.

questions.prompt: In this regression, what does βᵢ measure?
options: The systematic loss sensitivity of sector i's loans to losses on total loans
The sector's loss rate when it has no sensitivity to portfolio losses
The share of loans in sector i
questions.explanation: βᵢ > 1: sector losses move more than the portfolio's.
feedback: That's α.
That's a weight, not a sensitivity.
Recovery isn't in this model.
questions.equation: \frac{\text{Sectoral losses in sector } i}{\text{Loans to sector } i} = \alpha + \beta_i \left(\frac{\text{Total loan losses}}{\text{Total loans}}\right)

questions.prompt: A sector's βᵢ is estimated at 1.4. What should the bank conclude?
options: Sector losses rise faster than portfolio losses, so it's riskier and the bank should have less appetite to concentrate there
The sector is less sensitive than average
The sector has a 1.4% loss rate
The sector should get a higher concentration limit
questions.explanation: β above 1 means above-average systematic loss sensitivity.
feedback: That's β < 1.
β is a sensitivity, not a loss rate.
Higher β argues for a lower limit.

questions.prompt: A sector's estimated β rises above 1. What happens to the bank's appetite to concentrate lending there?
questions.explanation: Higher systematic loss sensitivity makes the sector riskier, so the bank should lend less there.
feedback: A higher β means more risk.
β is exactly what this model uses to judge sectors.

questions.prompt: Sector A has β = 0.8 and sector B has β = 1.5 (α = 0 for both). The total loan loss rate rises by 1 percentage point. What happens to each sector's loss rate?
options: A rises 0.8 points and B rises 1.5 points, so B's losses grow almost twice as fast
A rises 1.5 points and B 0.8 points
questions.explanation: Change in sector loss rate = βᵢ × change in total loss rate: 0.8 × 1 and 1.5 × 1.
feedback: That ignores β.
That swaps the betas.
α is the intercept; β drives the change.

concepts.name: Regulatory credit portfolio models
concepts.definition: Concentration limits were criticised as arbitrary; Basel II brought quantitative models: Moody's KMV (MPT), CreditMetrics (mark-to-market, VaR) and Credit Risk+ (default paradigm, expected losses and their distribution). The BIS sees benefits but warns that credit correlations are hard to estimate.
misconceptions: Mixing up CreditMetrics (mark-to-market) and Credit Risk+ (default mode)

questions.prompt: Which model uses a mark-to-market paradigm and estimates VaR on loans and loan portfolios?
questions.explanation: Mark-to-market: any change in a loan's value (upgrade, downgrade or default) counts, using rating transition matrices.
feedback: Credit Risk+ uses a default paradigm.
KMV applies MPT to loans.
Altman's Z is a scoring model.

questions.prompt: Credit Risk+ (CSFP) follows which paradigm?
options: Default paradigm: estimate expected default losses and their distribution to set the capital needed
questions.explanation: Like an insurer working out claim rates from historical default rates.
feedback: That's CreditMetrics.
That's KMV.
That's the term-structure approach from Week 5.

questions.prompt: Why did regulators move from concentration limits towards quantitative credit models?
options: Concentration limits were criticised for being arbitrary; Basel II led to greater reliance on models
Models remove the need for capital
Limits were too expensive to monitor
Models were required by deposit insurers
questions.explanation: Since the mid-2000s Basel II encouraged KMV, CreditMetrics and Credit Risk+.
feedback: Models help allocate capital; they don't remove it.
Cost isn't the reason given.
Not the reason given.

questions.prompt: According to the BIS, what is the main caveat to credit models reflecting risk concentration?
options: Credit correlations are extremely difficult to calculate and not well understood (e.g. sub-prime)
They can't be used for pricing
questions.explanation: If correlations are well understood, VaR gives one aggregate figure; sub-prime showed they weren't.
feedback: Not the caveat.
Better pricing of risk is listed as a benefit.
Not the caveat.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a benefit of credit models listed by the BIS?
options: Removing the need to hold economic capital
Assisting in better pricing of risk
A formal framework for allocating economic capital
questions.explanation: Models help allocate capital; they don't remove the need for it.
feedback: That's listed.
That's listed.
That's listed.

questions.prompt: A bank's model assumes mortgage defaults are far less correlated than they really are (as in sub-prime). What happens?
options: Portfolio risk and VaR are understated, so the bank holds too little capital and losses can exceed it
Portfolio risk is overstated, so the bank holds too much capital
Nothing, because correlation only affects return
questions.explanation: ρ too low → covariance terms too small → σp and VaR understated → capital too low → real losses overwhelm it.
feedback: Underestimating ρ makes risk look smaller, not larger.
Correlation affects risk, not expected return.
Correlation drives portfolio risk.

questions.prompt: A bank wants to measure how much a loan's value falls if the borrower is downgraded from A to BBB, even without a default. Which model fits?
options: CreditMetrics: its mark-to-market paradigm values upgrades and downgrades, not just defaults
Credit Risk+, because it models defaults
questions.explanation: Credit Risk+ only counts losses from default; CreditMetrics revalues the loan for any rating migration.
feedback: A default paradigm ignores downgrades without default.
That measures concentration against a benchmark.
Limits cap exposure; they don't value loans.
